blocks.text: A collection has at least three properties worth separating: how many elements are logically present, how much storage is available, and who owns that storage. Standard containers make those properties easier to manage, but they do not remove the need to understand them. HarborWorks will use a fixed calibration array and a growing sequence of readings to compare the two models.

reading.title: 12.1.1 Creating Type-Safe Fixed Arrays
paragraphs: std::array<T, N> is a standard container containing exactly N elements. Its extent is part of the type, so std::array<int, 4> and std::array<int, 5> are distinct types. It supports value copying, size queries, iterators, and checked access through at.

The elements reside within the array object rather than in a separately managed dynamic buffer. Where that object itself resides depends on its storage duration and ownership. A std::array can be a local variable, a class member, or part of a dynamically allocated object. Do not equate the container name with one physical memory region. A zero-element array is representable, but it has no element available to access.

std::array<T, N> represents a fixed number of elements through a standard-container interface. The element type and extent are part of its type. Unlike a raw array in many function parameter forms, the object carries its extent through its type and offers operations such as size, begin, end, and at.

For a small calibration table whose number of entries is a design constant, this is a natural choice. A std::array<int, 3> cannot become a four-element array by appending. If the requirement says the number of calibration values varies at runtime, that is a reason to choose another representation rather than to fight the fixed type.

Initialization still matters. A value-initialized array of integers has a known initial state. An uninitialized automatic array of fundamental values should not be read merely because it is wrapped in a standard type. The container interface does not erase the element type’s initialization rules.

A zero-extent std::array can represent a valid empty fixed collection. Iterating from begin to end performs no element work. Operations that require an existing element, such as accessing the first element, still need the relevant precondition. “The container object exists” is not the same as “an element exists.”

Ordinary value copying and assignment are available when the element type supports them. This makes the container easier to use as part of a structured value than a raw array with a separate informal size convention.

topics.title: 12.2.2 Understanding Size and Capacity
topics.summary: Size is the number of constructed elements available to the program. Capacity is the amount of element storage available before another reallocation is required. reserve(100) may provide capacity for at least 100 elements without creating them; accessing element 99 is still invalid until the size includes it. resize(100) changes the number of elements and initializes new ones as specified.

blocks.text: Capacity growth is an implementation strategy, not an exact doubling promise. A linear search for duplicate identifiers is acceptable at the teaching limit. Replacing it with a linked structure merely because insertion is possible would add allocation and pointer-management complexity without a demonstrated need.

blocks.text: Stable record identity should be modeled explicitly. An identifier belongs to the record; a vector index is a current position. If a later operation sorts or erases records, positions can change. This is a semantic issue even when all memory accesses remain within bounds.

topics.summary: Why does reserve not make indexing valid? It addresses allocation capacity, not the number of constructed elements in the vector’s logical sequence.

cards.question: Why does reserve not make indexing valid?
cards.answer: It addresses allocation capacity, not the number of constructed elements in the vector’s logical sequence.

cards.question: Why is exact capacity a poor portable assertion?
cards.answer: The interface permits implementation choices beyond the requested minimum. Correctness should depend on the guarantee the program actually needs.

cards.question: Why not delete data() manually?
cards.answer: The container owns that allocation. Manually releasing borrowed storage would violate the ownership model and corrupt later container behavior.

cards.question: Why can an index remain valid but become misleading?
cards.answer: Structural operations can move a different record into that position. Bounds validity does not establish stable identity.
